title: A single exceptional-component pushout on a nodal marked curve
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field] [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $(R,L)$ and $(C,D)$ be semistable multipointed $k$-curves [def-trf-multipointed-curve] [def-trf-multipointed-curve-modification], with no properness, separatedness or connectedness assumed for their structural maps to $k$. Let $r:(R,L)\to(C,D)$ be a proper surjective morphism of pairs [def-weil-proper-morphism], whose marking map is an isomorphism. Assume all geometric fibres [def-weil-geometric-fibre] of its curve map are connected [def-weil-connected-scheme]. Suppose $U\subset C$ is an open subset meeting every irreducible component [def-weil-irreducible-components] of $C$ and $r^{-1}(U)\to U$ is an isomorphism. Let $A\subset R$ be an irreducible component isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1_k$ [def-sc-p1-standard], mapped by $r$ to one point, such that the boundary $\partial_R A=A\cap\overline{R\setminus A}$ is nonempty and $|A\cap(L\cup R_{\mathrm{sing}})|\le2$. The singular locus here is the set of points where $R/k$ is not smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Then the scheme pushout [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit] of $R\leftarrow A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] exists. Its map $h:R\to R_1$ is proper and surjective, has connected geometric fibres, contracts precisely $A$ and is an isomorphism $R\setminus A\simeq R_1\setminus\{h(A)\}$. The scheme-theoretic image $L_1$ of $L$ (defined by the kernel of $\mathcal O_{R_1}\to h_*\mathcal O_L$) gives a semistable multipointed pair $(R_1,L_1)$ and $L\to L_1$ is an isomorphism. The factorization $r=r_1h$ induced by the pushout is a proper surjective morphism of pairs to $(C,D)$ with connected geometric curve fibres, marking map an isomorphism, and $r_1^{-1}(U)\simeq U$. The irreducible components of $R_1$ are exactly the images of the components of $R$ other than $A$, with distinct such components having distinct images.

proof.text: A chosen algebraic closure $\iota:k\to\bar k$ is an isomorphism, since $k$ is algebraically closed and every element of $\bar k$ has a linear minimal polynomial over $\iota(k)$; so the geometric fibre of $R\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is $R$ itself up to $\iota$, and semistability says that every point of $R$ is smooth over $k$ or has completed local ring $k[[u,v]]/(uv)$. Hence $R$ is reduced by [lem-trf-nodal-points-reduced-algebraically-closed] (it is of finite type over $k$, being finitely presented). Give $A$ its reduced closed-subcurve structure and put $B=\overline{R\setminus A}_{\mathrm{red}}$. Applying [lem-trf-nodal-subcurve-boundary] (with $N=R$) to $A$ gives $E=A\cap B$ finite reduced, with every point a node of $R$ and smooth on both subcurves. Applying it to $B$ also proves that $B$ is nodal at its closed points. $B$ is a closed subscheme of the Noetherian finite-type $k$-scheme $R$, hence of finite presentation and flat over $k$, and it is pure of dimension one as the union of the components of $R$ other than $A$. Each generic point $\eta$ of $B$ lies in the open $R\setminus A$, on which the ideal of $A$ is the unit ideal, so $B$ and $R$ agree as open subschemes there and $B$ is smooth at $\eta$ because $R$ is. Thus every point of $B$ is smooth or an ordinary double point, and $(B,\varnothing)$ is a semistable multipointed $k$-curve. The ideals of $A$ and $B$ intersect to zero: a section in their intersection vanishes on all irreducible components and $R$ is reduced. Hence [lem-trf-closed-union-pushout] gives $R=A\amalg_E B$. The set $E$ is the stipulated nonempty boundary. Its points lie in $R_{\mathrm{sing}}$, so $d=|E|$ is $1$ or $2$. As $L$ avoids the singular locus, $|L\cap A|+d\le2$. Finally $B\to C$ is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-proper].

proof.text: The restriction $r|_A$ factors through a $k$-point $c:\operatorname{Spec}k\to C$. For an explicit check choose an affine neighbourhood $V=\operatorname{Spec}H$ of its singleton image. On the two standard charts of $A\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$ in [def-sc-p1-standard], the pullback of any $a\in H$ is a polynomial in $t$ and a polynomial in $t^{-1}$ with equal Laurent-polynomial restrictions. Only constants have both forms. These constants define a $k$-algebra map $H\to k$, and its composite with the chart inclusions gives exactly $r|_A$. The affine-spectrum functoriality in [def-weil-affine-spectrum] proves the factorization, including equality of morphisms rather than just equality of point images. In particular the restrictions of $B\to C$ and $c$ agree on $E$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-relative-nodal-point-pinching] to the proper map $B\to C$, the smooth closed set $E\subset B$, the one-point scheme $F=\operatorname{Spec}k$, and its map $c$ to $C$. All fibres of $E\to F$ have size $d\in\{1,2\}$. It gives $R_1=B\amalg_E F$, finite surjective $v:B\to R_1$, a closed point $y=F\subset R_1$ with $v^{-1}(y)=E$, the isomorphism $B\setminus E\simeq R_1\setminus\{y\}$, a semistable curve $R_1$, and a proper map $r_1:R_1\to C$. The maps $A\to F\to R_1$ and $v$ agree on $E$, so the closed-union pushout gives $h:R\to R_1$ and $r=r_1h$. For any target $T$, a pair $R\to T,F\to T$ agreeing on $A$ is, by $R=A\amalg_E B$, exactly a pair $B\to T,F\to T$ agreeing on $E$. The latter pair extends uniquely by the pinching pushout. This proves the required pushout universal property in schemes.

proof.text: The map $h$ is surjective since $v=h|_B$ is. Its complement of $A$ is $B\setminus E$, giving precisely the claimed isomorphism off $y$. It is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated]: use base $C$, proper $R\to C$, and separated $R_1\to C$ (the latter is proper by the pinching theorem). To check geometric fibres, the closed subcurves $A,B$ cover $R$, and after any field base change they still cover: every point maps to a point in one of the two closed subcurves. Over $y$, the pullback from $B$ is $E$ scheme-theoretically by the pinching theorem and is already contained in the pullback of $A$. Thus the closed immersion $A_\Omega\hookrightarrow h^{-1}(y)_\Omega$ is surjective on points and is a homeomorphism. Its underlying space is that of $\mathbf P^1_\Omega$, connected since the two integral affine-line charts have nonempty intersection. Away from $y$ the geometric fibres are single points by the complement isomorphism. This proves connectedness of every geometric fibre; it does not require any assertion about the fibre's nilpotent structure.

proof.text: The marking $L$ is a finite disjoint union of $k$-points. Indeed it is quasi-compact and etale over $k$; on every affine chart [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-over-field-product] makes its ring a finite product of finite separable extensions, all equal to $k$. Thus these singleton affine opens give the asserted finite discrete reduced scheme. Put $m=|L\cap A|$. The pinching theorem makes $y$ smooth if $d=1$, and a node if $d=2$. In the first case $m\le1$; in the second $m=0$. All markings off $A$ avoid $E$ and are carried by the complement isomorphism to distinct smooth points off $y$. If $m=1$, the unique marking on $A$ maps to the smooth point $y$, distinct from those other images. Hence $h|_L$ identifies $L$ with the reduced closed union of these distinct smooth $k$-points. To see closedness, each such point off $y$ is the finite-map image under $v$ of a closed marked point of $B$; $y$ itself is closed by pinching. On a neighbourhood of each image point, evaluation of regular functions onto its residue field $k$ is surjective, and the kernel cuts out that reduced point. Off the finite image the kernel is the unit ideal. Therefore this closed immersion has exactly the kernel ideal $\ker(\mathcal O_{R_1}\to h_*\mathcal O_L)$ specified in the item, so its image is $L_1$. It follows that $L\simeq L_1$ and $(R_1,L_1)$ is semistable.

proof.text: The maps on markings define a morphism of pairs $r_1:(R_1,L_1)\to(C,D)$: use $L\simeq L_1$ and the original marking map. Its marking map is an isomorphism by the hypothesis $L\simeq D$. Properness of $r_1$ was part of the pinching theorem, and surjectivity follows from $r=r_1h$. For any geometric point $\bar c\to C$, [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change] gives a surjection $R_{\bar c}\to(R_1)_{\bar c}$. The source is connected by hypothesis; if the target split into two nonempty clopen sets their inverse images would split the source, a contradiction. Thus $r_1$ has connected geometric fibres as claimed.

proof.text: Write $c=r(A)$. If $c$ belonged to $U$, then the fibre over $c$ of the isomorphism $r^{-1}(U)\to U$ would contain $A$, whereas that fibre is a point. Thus $c\notin U$, $y\notin r_1^{-1}(U)$, and restricting the complement isomorphism for $h$ identifies $r_1^{-1}(U)\to U$ with the original isomorphism. For irreducible components, $B$ is the reduced union of the components of $R$ other than $A$. Each has a generic point off $E$: $E$ is finite and consists of closed smooth points of $B$. The complement isomorphism for the finite surjection $v:B\to R_1$ bijects these generic points with those of $R_1$; no component of the pure one-dimensional curve $R_1$ is supported on $y$. Taking closures gives exactly the images of those components, since $v$ is closed. Distinct generic points remain distinct under the isomorphism, so their component images are distinct. Each such component has positive-dimensional image. Together with $h(A)=y$, this proves that $h$ contracts precisely $A$.
